background.definition: The pericardium is a double-walled sac, made up of the fibrous pericardium and serous pericardium that surrounds the heart. Pericardial effusion is an abnormal collection of fluid within this sac, which normally is lubricated with less than 30 mL of fluid.

list.listitem: A prospective study in emergency department patients complaining of dyspnea found that 14/103 had pericardial effusion (13.6%; 95% CI, 8%-23%).

Studies of subgroups found a prevalence of pericardial effusion of 13% in AIDS patients with cardiac manifestations, 1.5% to 22% in cardiac post-operative patients, 15% to 28% of patients with acute MI, and 23% in patients with malignancy.
In 60% of the patients, the cause of pericardial effusion is a known medical condition.
Malignancy: may be primary neoplasm (rare) or secondary spread (metastasis). Either condition may cause obstruction of the lymphatic drainage of the fluid, or an increase in fluid production.

HIV with or without AIDS: often due inflammatory response secondary to opportunistic infections, such as mycobacterial disease. However, most pericardial effusions in AIDS patients are idiopathic and asymptomatic.

Acute myocardial infarction (AMI): effusion occurs secondary to inflammatory response, and is generally larger if more cardiac tissue is involved (i.e., transmural AMIs develop large pericardial effusions).

Iatrogenic: Generally seen after cardiothoracic surgery and occurs due to both collection of blood and inflammatory fluids. Risk factors for effusion post-operatively in children include history of previous cardiac surgery, use of cardiopulmonary bypass, and longer duration of CPAP post-op.
Corticosteroid use for pericarditis increases the risk of effusion (OR 10.4; 95% CI, 4.5-24).
There is no evidence to support screening for pericardial effusions.
One opinion statement recommends that all HIV patients undergo periodic cardiac echocardiogram to evaluate for cardiac function. C

list.listitem: Patients suspected of pericardial effusion may present with breathlessness, chest pain, dyspnea on exertion, cough, and abdominal pain. Less common are fever, chills, and night sweats. Data from well-designed clinical diagnostic studies are lacking, though, so estimates of sensitivity and specificity are unknown.

Consider comorbid conditions when suspecting pericardial effusion; often, treating the underlying condition will resolve the effusion. A systematic review found that the five symptoms in patients with pericardial effusion that predict tamponade were dyspnea, tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, elevated jugular venous pressure, and cardiomegaly on chest radiograph.

When symptoms are suggestive, diagnosis should start with ECG which may demonstrate diminished QRS and T-wave voltages, PR-segment depression, ST-T changes, bundle branch block, and electrical alternans ().

If ECG is indeterminate or suggestive, a CXR may be performed. This may demonstrate “pseudo”-cardiomegaly () Echocardiography () may be performed. There are several grades of effusion based on the Horowitz classification: (1) small (echo-free space in diastole <10 mm), (2) moderate (10–20 mm),(3) large (>20 mm), and (4) very large (>20 mm and compression of the heart). Adenosine deaminase (ADA) is a useful test for diagnosis of tuberculous pericarditis (sensitivity 88%, specificity 83%, LR+ 5.2, LR– 0.14).
Ultrasound findings of cardiac tamponade include Right Atrial/Ventricular compression during diastole, and Inferior Vena Cava plethoar.
All patients with acute pericarditis should undergo transthoracic echocardiography to assess effusion size and identify potential complications.
Suspect pericardial effusion in patients with dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, fever (especially if malignancy, recent cardiac surgery, or HIV).
Bedside ultrasound can quickly identify pericardial effusion and screen for cardiac tamponade
NSAIDs including aspirin remain the usual first-line agent for small pericardial effusions, although evidence of effectiveness is mixed, and one RCT found no benefit.B

Pericardiocentesis is not necessary when the effusions are small and will resolve under anti-inflammatory treatment. Surgical treatment should be reserved for patients with hemodynamic compromise or large, chronic effusions using ultrasound or CT guidance.B
Pericardial fluid should be drained slowly to prevent pericardial decompression syndrome. C

Evidence for the use of NSAIDs, such as aspirin, is weak. However, they remain the preferred first line agent for treating small pericardial effusions secondary to pericarditis or of unknown etiology.

One multi-center, double-blinded RCT with 196 patients found no significant reduction in the grade of post-operative pericardial effusions with the use of NSAIDs versus placebo (RR −0.28; 95% CI, −0.63 to 0.06; p = 0.105).

Aspirin should be administered 750 to 100 mg TID for 1 to 2 weeks for first episode and 2 to 4 weeks for recurrent episodes. For Ibuprofen, the dosage is 600 mg TID for 1 to 2 weeks for first episode and 2 to 4 weeks for recurrent episodes.

Colchicine has been shown in a prospective, open label RCT to reduce symptoms as well as decrease effusion size in patients suffering from a first episode of acute pericarditis (n = 120; recurrence rate at 18 months 10.7%; p = 0.004; NNT = 5). Colchicine should be administered as 0.5 mg BID for 3 months in first episode, and 6 to 12 months in recurrent episodes.

However, two trials in patients with a pleural effusion following cardiac surgery failed to find a beneit of colchicine administration. One randomized 197 patients with moderate to large sized effusion to colchicine or p lacebo, with no difference in outcomes or late tamponade. A second randomized 149 patients with asymptomatic mild or moderate post-operative pericardial effusion, and found no benefit.
Surgical treatment is reserved for cases of hemodynamic compromise and chronic large pericardial effusions.
When performing surgical treatment for hemodynamic compromise, both ultrasound and CT-guided pericardiocentesis have been shown to be a safe and effective means of relieving tamponade.
A surgical pleuro-pericardial window is recommended only in patients with very large and chronic effusions for which repeated pericardiocentesis and/or intrapericardial therapy were not successful.

A retrospective study of 64 cases of pericardial effusion found that choice of operative intervention should be based on etiology of pericardial effusion.This study found that pericardiocentesis is best for acute pericardial effusions with tamponade.

Pleuro-percardial window via VATS is preferred for chronic pericardial effusions secondary to infective or systemic disease and in recurrence after subxiphoid drainage. Subxipoid drainage is best for all neoplastic causes of effusions, and for idiopathic cases in order to perform pericardioscopy.
Pericardial fluid should be drained slowly to prevent pericardial decompression syndrome.

Emerging evidence indicates that idiopathic, chronic (>3 months), and large (>2 cm) asymptomatic pericardial effusions generally follow a benign course, supporting watchful waiting as a more appropriate and cost-effective strategy..
Natural history of pericardial effusion may include accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac to the point of ventricular collapse and finally tamponade of the heart leading to death.
A prospective observational study of 453 patients found that signs of poor prognosis include fever >38°C, subacute course, large effusion or tamponade, and aspirin or NSAID failure.B
For patients requiring drainage of pericardial effusions, those who had extended drainage of 2 to 3 days with catheter placement have a decreased chance of recurrence.B
A moderate to large pericardial effusion is a marker of poor outcome in patients with ST elevation myocardial infarction, malignancy, heart failure, and pulmonary artery hypertension.
A lung cancer with pericardial effusion has poor prognosis
In most cases of cardiac tamponade, a moderate to large pericardial effusion exists. In trauma, a small amount of fluid can trigger tamponade.
Pericardial effusions, especially if large, is worrisome because of possible progression to cardiac tamponade.
